description: DeltaE76, DeltaE94 and DeltaEok. Fewer published reference values exist for these than for CIEDE2000, so the set leans on definitional anchors and on two properties that are themselves published: CIEDE2000's symmetry, which appears in the Sharma-Wu-Dalal data as pairs 7 and 8 being the same colours reversed with the same answer, and DeltaE94's ASYMMETRY, which is specified rather than accidental.

entries.source: CIE 1994 (CIE 116-1995), graphic-arts application: kL = 1, K1 = 0.045, K2 = 0.015
CIE 1994 (CIE 116-1995), textiles application: kL = 2, K1 = 0.048, K2 = 0.014
CIE 1976 — a Euclidean distance in CIELAB, so white to black is the L* range
CIE 142:2001 — at Lbar' = 50 the lightness compensation Sl is exactly 1, and a pure lightness difference has no chroma or hue term, so DeltaE00 equals DeltaE76 here
Sharma, Wu & Dalal (2005), pairs 7 and 8 — the same two colours in both orders, both published as 2.3669
CIE 1994 — Sc and Sh are computed from the FIRST colour, which the standard calls the reference
entries.derivationNote: Lab1 = [60.2574, -34.0099, 36.2677], Lab2 = [60.4626, -34.1751, 39.4387]. Forward gives 1.3909947095, reversed gives 1.3576187101 — a 2.4% difference. Recorded as an entry because it looks like a defect: a caller ranking candidates must pass the reference consistently, or the ordering means nothing.

entries.source: Sharma, Wu & Dalal (2005) pair 1, measured under both metrics
entries.derivationNote: DeltaE76 = 4.0010632837 against a published DeltaE00 of 2.0425 for the same pair — a factor of 1.9589. This is why CIE 142 exists, and why DeltaE76 is never a stated result here.

entries.source: A Euclidean distance is zero exactly when the operands are equal
Ottosson (2020) — OKLab lightness is on [0,1], so the white-to-black distance is 1, NOT 100
